content: This disease is geographically distributed in Asia and the Indian subcontinent, particularly in regions where humans raise pigs and consume raw aquatic plants. The infection cycle begins when the parasite infects an amphibic snail, such as Segmentina nitidella, Segmentina hemisphaerula, Hippeutis schmackeri, Gyraulus, Lymnaea, Pila, or Planorbis (Indoplanorbis), after being released through infected feces. From this intermediate host, the metacercariae attach to aquatic plants, which are subsequently ingested raw by pigs and humans. Additionally, water can become a source of infection if consumed unheated, as encysted cercariae are not only present on aquatic plants but also on the surface of the water. Clinically, most infections are mild and asymptomatic. However, in cases of heavier infection, symptoms may include diarrhea, abdominal pain, fever, ascites, anasarca, and intestinal obstruction. Laboratory diagnosis relies on the microscopic identification of eggs, or less commonly, adult flukes, in stool or vomitus samples. The eggs are morphologically indistinguishable from those of Fasciola hepatica. The treatment of choice for fasciolopsiasis is praziquantel. The incidence and prevalence of this disease are significant, with an estimated 10 million people in East Asia potentially infected with this fluke. Despite this, its radiological identification has not been reported. Photomicrographs of fecal samples have revealed the presence of various parasitic worm eggs, including those of the trematode Fasciolopsis buski, as well as nematodes such as Ascaris species, Trichuris species, and an unidentified species of nematodal hookworm.
